question: For those looking to navigate through the complicated world of EU funding, dozens of university degrees such as a ‘Masters in EU Project Design and Management’ and four-semester courses with tuition fees of up to EUR 8 000 are now being offered across the EU.

Furthermore, consultancy groups like EY, PwC, KPMG and Deloitte and Roche, which also like to employ retired Commission officials, and hundreds of small companies on the ‘European Register of EU Project Designers’, advertise their services to help people apply for EU funding in return for success fees. 1.

When and how will the Commission make it simpler to apply for funding so that even ordinary mortals, like university lecturers, farmers, regional officials or entrepreneurs, can complete the process themselves within 48 hours and stand a chance of success?

How much do applicants end up spending per application and per funding year because of the Commission’s hyper-complex application and reporting obligations, including the processing fees and the success fees charged by consultants?
answer: The Funding & Tender Opportunities Portal (1) offers information on accessing EU funding initiatives implemented by the Commission. The portal provides instructions on available EU funding programmes, how to apply online, and information on financial instruments such as guarantees, loans.

The Financial Regulation (2) includes the rules and principles governing EU grants, including the principle of equal treatment (3), aiming to ensure that everyone has equal access to EU funding and information. The same principles apply to EU funds managed at national or regional levels.
Transparent procedures mean that calls for proposals are published on the mentioned portal, specifying all conditions for applying for the funding and the supporting documents required.

The Financial Regulation has streamlined access to EU funding, requiring beneficiaries to provide less detailed information, which will be further streamlined with a view to reducing bureaucracy for ‘very low value grants’, as introduced in the recently agreed recast of the Financial Regulation.

Another example is the legal entity validation, which has been simplified and made a one-time process to facilitate ongoing and future applications without re-registration. The use of consultants is not necessary for the application and evaluation process for EU funding opportunities.

As per the Financial Regulation, even in cases where the Commission needs the assistance of external experts during the evaluation process, the costs for the experts’ remuneration are covered by the EU budget and not by the applicants (4). The Commission has made great efforts to simplify its procedures to ensure a level playing field for all applicants.
As EU funding is limited, competition can be significant and applicants may engage external support. This is however not a requirement for presenting applications for EU funding.
